source: Knuth and Moore (1975) alpha-beta pruning; McCarthy; Brudno (1963) (history via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Alpha-beta was invented several times (McCarthy, Brudno 1963). Knuth and Moore (1975) refined and analysed it. It returns the same value as minimax but skips branches that cannot change the result.
numbers: Worst case O(b^d), same as minimax. Best case with perfect move ordering about O(b^(d/2)): search twice as deep for the same work.
quote: Newell and Simon 1958: alpha-beta 'appears to have been reinvented a number of times'.
limits: Gain depends wholly on move ordering (captures, killer moves, iterative deepening). Secondary source only; the Knuth-Moore paper itself was not opened (PDF fetch returned empty).
agent_relevance: Pruning is exact only when the evaluation is exact. Our S6 tree search has a noisy model evaluator, so hard alpha-beta cuts are unsafe; soft pruning by code-counted checks is safer.

source: Campbell, Hoane, Hsu (2002) Deep Blue; match facts via Wikipedia
finding: Deep Blue was brute-force alpha-beta search on custom chips with a hand-built evaluation. It won the 1997 rematch against Kasparov.
numbers: 1997 match 3.5-2.5 (2 wins, 3 draws, 1 loss for Deep Blue). 1996 match lost 2-4. About 200 million positions per second in 1997 (about double 1996). 30 PowerPC 604e processors plus 480 chess chips. Evaluation about 8,000 parts. Opening book over 4,000 positions and 700,000 GM games. Typical depth 6 to 8 moves, 20 or more in some lines. Levy and Newborn: each extra ply worth about 50-70 Elo.
limits: Secondary source. The original 2002 Artificial Intelligence paper was blocked (HTTP 403), so opened is for the Wikipedia summary only. Single match of 6 games; game-2 bug controversy.
agent_relevance: Strength came from search volume plus large human-written knowledge. An LLM agent has very low node throughput, so it cannot copy brute force; it must prune with a prior.

source: Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning (UCT)
finding: UCT applies the UCB1 bandit rule at every tree node so rollouts concentrate on promising moves. It is proved consistent: failure probability goes to zero.
numbers: P-game trees (B=2,D=20 and B=8,D=8), 200 trees x 200 runs each: UCT reaches near-zero failure in about as many leaf nodes as alpha-beta, and is faster if a small failure rate is accepted. Iterations needed grow about B^(D/2), like alpha-beta. Plain Monte Carlo plateaus at a significant error rate.
quote: in several domains, UCT is significantly more efficient than its alternatives
limits: Artificial random trees and a sailing MDP, not real games. The bias term was modified by depth to get this result. Alpha-beta assumed to pick randomly if stopped early.
agent_relevance: UCT is anytime: stop at any budget and take the best-visited move. Fits a token budget at S6. The exploration constant needs testing on our tasks.

source: Browne et al. (2012) A survey of Monte Carlo tree search methods
finding: Survey of the first five years of MCTS: four phases (selection, expansion, simulation, backpropagation), UCT, many enhancements (RAVE/AMAF, parallelisation, MCTS-Solver) and applications.
numbers: Timeline in survey: 2006 Gelly et al. apply UCT to Go (MoGo); 2008 MoGo reaches dan (master) level on 9x9 Go. As of 2011 top computer Go programs all used MCTS and played at the strength of a good amateur on 19x19.
limits: Cut-off October 2011, before deep nets. Plain random-rollout MCTS is weak on tactically sharp games such as chess.
agent_relevance: MCTS has a standard vocabulary and menu of known fixes (solver, progressive widening) that can be mapped to scaffold operators.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm (AlphaZero preprint)
finding: One algorithm (self-play RL, policy+value net, MCTS) reached superhuman chess, shogi and Go from rules alone, with no human data and no handcrafted evaluation.
numbers: Chess 100-game match at 1 min/move vs Stockfish: 28 wins, 72 draws, 0 losses (White 25W 25D 0L; Black 3W 47D 0L). Shogi vs Elmo: 90W, 2D, 8L. Go vs 3-day AlphaGo Zero: 60W 40L. Chess passed Stockfish after about 4 h (300k steps); 700k steps total; 800 MCTS simulations per move in training; 5,000 first-gen TPUs for self-play and 64 TPUs to train.
quote: AlphaZero searches just 80 thousand positions per second in chess ... compared to 70 million for Stockfish
limits: Stockfish ran at 64 threads, 1 GB hash, fixed time per move, no opening book: criticised as handicapped. Draws compress the chess Elo scale. One lab's own match.
agent_relevance: Search 1000x thinner but guided by a learned prior wins. Fits the schema idea: fewer well-chosen branches beat wide blind search.

source: AlphaZero Science (2018) 1000-game match and criticism (via Wikipedia)
finding: The longer match in Science used more neutral conditions and AlphaZero still won clearly, by a smaller share.
numbers: 1,000 games vs Stockfish 9 dev: AlphaZero 155 wins, 6 losses, 839 draws. Conditions: 3 h + 15 s per move, Stockfish with 44 cores, Syzygy tables, 32 GB hash. Reported that Stockfish needed about 10-to-1 time odds to match. Preprint critics: Romstad said fixed time and 1 GB hash hurt Stockfish; Kaufman said an opening book would narrow the gap.
limits: Secondary source; last 20% of the page not read. Later Stockfish NNUE and Leela Chess Zero reached parity, and Stockfish later pulled ahead (no numbers on the page).
agent_relevance: The headline edge survived a fairer re-test, but the margin changed from 28-0 to about 15.5% wins. Re-test striking edges under fair compute.

source: Silver et al. (2016, 2017) AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero (match facts via Wikipedia pages)
finding: AlphaGo Zero dropped human game data: net-guided MCTS self-play alone beat all earlier AlphaGo versions.
numbers: AlphaGo Zero beat AlphaGo Lee 100-0 and AlphaGo Master 89-11. Passed Lee in 3 days (about 4.9 million self-play games), Master level in 21 days, all previous versions at 40 days. Earlier AlphaGo: 5-0 over Fan Hui (Oct 2015), 4-1 over Lee Sedol (March 2016).
limits: Secondary summaries; the Nature papers were not opened. Lee Sedol's game-4 win exposed a failure: AlphaGo estimated about 70% at move 79, its estimate collapsed at move 87, and it played bad moves 87-101.
agent_relevance: Search value estimates can be badly wrong on rare tactical lines. An outside verifier is needed; a self-estimated win chance is not proof (G2/G3).

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2019) MuZero: Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model
finding: MuZero plans with MCTS over a learned model (value, policy, reward only) without being given the rules, and matches AlphaZero.
numbers: Matched AlphaZero in chess, shogi and Go with 800 simulations per move; 50 simulations per move in Atari. Atari, 57 games: MuZero Reanalyze 731% median human-normalised score vs 192%, 231%, 431% for previous methods. Used 16 residual blocks vs AlphaZero's 20 yet matched it.
limits: Learned model predicts only planning-relevant quantities. Reported by the authors only.
agent_relevance: A model acting as its own world model is the LLM analogue. Require only that rollouts predict what the checks need, not a perfect simulator.

source: Jones (2021) Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games
finding: Using AlphaZero on Hex, train-time compute and test-time search trade off in a clean log-linear way.
numbers: Each extra 10x of train-time compute lets you cut about 15x of test-time compute with performance unchanged, down to a floor of a single-node search. Larger test-time tree searches substantially improve the agent. Performance at fixed compute degrades predictably as the board grows.
quote: for each additional 10x of train-time compute, about 15x of test-time compute can be eliminated
limits: One game (Hex), small boards, AlphaZero only. The author notes it may be a property unique to Hex.
agent_relevance: Early evidence for test-time compute scaling in a search agent. With a frozen model our only lever is test-time search, so expect the floor effect to bind.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Grandmaster-Level Chess Without Search
finding: A 270M transformer trained by supervised learning on 10M Lichess games annotated with Stockfish 16 action-values plays at grandmaster level with no search.
numbers: Dataset: 15.3B action-values (about 530M board states). 270M model: tournament Elo 2299, Lichess blitz 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots, puzzle accuracy 95.4%. 9M model: 2025 Elo, 88.9% puzzles. 136M: 2259, 94.5%. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct: 1755 vs bots, 66.5% puzzles.
limits: Elo falls against bots. Fischer random chess drops to 1539 (vs bots), so it relies on the training distribution. It is distillation of an engine, with the oracle needed for labels.
agent_relevance: Search can be amortised into a policy. Cached good move-sets (case memory) may replace some search, but only in familiar distributions.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) searchless chess: comparison with AlphaZero and Leela (Table 1)
finding: Shows how much search adds to RL engines when tested with and without MCTS.
numbers: Tournament Elo: AlphaZero policy-only 1777, value-only 1992, 400 MCTS sims 2470. Leela Chess Zero policy-only 2292, value-only 2418, 400 sims 2858. Stockfish 16 at 50 ms 2711; at 1.5 s 2935. Puzzle accuracy: AlphaZero 56.1 / 82.0 / 95.6%; Leela 88.6 / 95.9 / 99.6%.
limits: Internal tournament Elo, not comparable to Lichess Elo (paper says so). Different training sets for AlphaZero and Leela.
agent_relevance: Search added about 690 Elo to AlphaZero's policy net and about 570 to Leela's. Search over a good net is worth several hundred rating points.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) searchless chess: generalisation limit
finding: Limits of a searchless distilled policy.
numbers: Fischer random chess: 1539 Elo vs bots, versus 2054 for the 9M-sized agent in standard chess against bots. Against bots the 270M model scores 2299, against humans 2895.
limits: Distribution shift hurts; no search to repair errors in new positions.
agent_relevance: Amortised intuition breaks off-distribution; search or checks are the fallback. Good trigger for an impasse signal at S6.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models
finding: An LLM (MAV, multi-action-value) is trained as policy, value and world model; used inside MCTS (external) or trained on linearised search trees (internal), reaching grandmaster-level chess.
numbers: MAV alone: external Elo 2923 (mean scoring) or 2875 (max scoring). MAV+MCTS with 100 simulations: internal Elo 68 above MAV alone; Elo rises roughly logarithmically with simulations; about +300 Elo even with limited search. Legal-move and next-state accuracy about 0.996-1.000 on Lichess puzzles and random out-of-distribution boards. Games played: 14,689 chess, 4,480 Chess960, 2,189 Connect Four, 6,334 Hex. Only 10% of evaluated positions were in training data.
quote: search-based planning can yield significant improvements in LLM game-playing strength
limits: External Elos of MCTS agents are anchored to blitz Stockfish levels; the authors say they are not accurate. In Hex a game engine supplied the legal moves. Game data only, no natural language. Needs engine-annotated data.
agent_relevance: Best direct test of search with an LLM in games: search helps, logarithmic in budget, and state-tracking MCTS skips hallucinated states by design.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) internal search results (same paper)
finding: Internal search: the model writes a minimax tree of set breadth and depth in one call; strength rises with token budget.
numbers: Breadth up to 4, depth up to 2. External Elo rose with test-time tokens from about 2870 (MAV alone) to about 2930. The requested tree shape was produced in 99.6% of 5,980 positions. Worked example: first answer qd6, after exploring top-3 lines one step further the model switched to qXg6.
limits: Gains smaller than external MCTS. Depth only 2. The self-correction example is a single illustration. Elo values read from a figure.
agent_relevance: A model can learn to run search in its own context, and code can check the tree shape. Supports code deciding tree shape (section 1 of the schema).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Treat reasoning as search over thoughts: the model proposes thoughts and scores states; code runs BFS or DFS with a beam.
numbers: Game of 24 (100 games, GPT-4): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%; CoT best-of-100 49%. About 60% of CoT samples already failed after the first step.
quote: while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%
limits: Game of 24 is shallow (3 steps) with a clean checker. Value scores come from the same model prompting itself. Feng et al. show prompted values are weak.
agent_relevance: Beam search works when steps are small and checkable. The model-as-value part is the fragile piece (G5).

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: The LLM acts as world model and policy inside MCTS, with a reward from self-evaluation.
numbers: Blocksworld with LLaMA-33B (2/4/6-step): CoT 0.17, 0.02, 0.00; RAP(20 iterations) 1.00, 0.88, 0.42. Average RAP success 64%; paper reports a 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT. GSM8k: CoT 29.4%, CoT+SC(10) 46.8%, RAP(1) 48.6%, RAP(10) 51.6%.
limits: Blocksworld has a small state space; 42% at 6 steps leaves most cases failing. On GSM8k the gap to CoT+SC(10) is small (48.6 vs 46.8 at RAP(1)).
agent_relevance: World-model rollouts beat left-to-right on long plans. Success shrinks with depth, so depth limits must be explicit.

source: Feng et al. (2024) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide LLM Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: A learned value function with AlphaZero-style MCTS beats prompted value functions on LLM reasoning, and works on long-horizon tasks (RLHF, chess endgame) where ToT and RAP fail.
numbers: Prompted vs learned value (ToT-BFS Path@1, rows from text extraction): LLaMA-SFT policy 9.2% (prompted LLaMA), 21.0% (prompted GPT-3.5), 64.8% (learned LLaMA-V) on one task; GPT-3.5 policy 15.5% vs 19.1%. Game24-type row: 37.4 / 45.8 / 52.5. GSM8K: 72.7 vs 74.0. MCTS-alpha and MCTS-Rollout clearly beat BFS/DFS on long-horizon tasks and match them on shallow trees.
limits: The PDF text extraction garbled the table, so row-to-task alignment is approximate; use the direction, not the exact figures. Needs a trained value net, which we cannot do.
agent_relevance: Prompted self-evaluation is a weak value signal. Without training, use code checks or held-out tests instead (G3, G5).

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Searchformer
finding: A transformer trained on A* search traces, then bootstrapped to shorter traces, solves planning tasks in fewer search steps than A*.
numbers: Sokoban: solves 93.7% of unseen puzzles optimally while using up to 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* used for training. Beats solution-only baselines with 5-10x smaller model size and 10x smaller training set.
limits: Small grid tasks with an exact oracle. Table garbled in extraction, so only abstract numbers used.
agent_relevance: Teaching a model the search procedure can beat answer-only prediction. Not available to a frozen-model scaffold.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs (KataGo)
finding: Adversarial policies trained against KataGo win without playing Go well; search does not remove the weakness.
numbers: Win rate >99% vs KataGo with no search and >97% vs superhuman search settings. Pass-adversary: 100% over 1,048 games vs no-search. Cyclic-adversary: 95.7% vs Latest-def at 4,096 visits; 72% vs Latest at 10 million visits. Used under 14% of KataGo's training compute. Human experts can copy the strategy to beat several superhuman AIs. Weakness persists after adversarial training.
quote: our adversaries do not win by playing Go well
limits: Aimed at KataGo; transfers zero-shot to other superhuman Go AIs.
agent_relevance: Superhuman average strength does not give worst-case robustness, even with MCTS. A scaffold needs adversarial test inputs, not only typical ones.

source: Wang et al. (2023) KataGo adversarial: effect of search on the exploit
finding: More search lowers the adversary's win rate but does not remove it.
numbers: Cyclic adversary win rate 95.7% at 4,096 victim visits, 72% at 10 million visits. Appendix E.2 estimate: the victim at 4,096 visits is already far stronger than top human Go players.
limits: The exploit targets a group-status misjudgement that the value net shares with the search.
agent_relevance: Search shares the value network's blind spot. Independent checks beat deeper search with the same evaluator (G4).

source: Wu (2019) Accelerating Self-Play Learning in Go (KataGo)
finding: Efficiency changes to AlphaZero-style training cut compute greatly.
numbers: 50x reduction in compute over comparable methods. KataGo passes ELF OpenGo after 19 days on about 27 V100 GPUs (about 1.4 GPU-years) vs about 74 GPU-years for ELF (2000 V100 GPUs, 13-14 days) and about 41 TPU-years for AlphaZero's Go run.
limits: Some gains are Go-specific (ownership and score targets); the general ones transfer.
agent_relevance: AlphaZero-style cost was largely avoidable, but self-play search still needs training; we use search without training.

source: Why MCTS beat alpha-beta in Go but not chess (Browne 2012 plus AlphaZero 2017)
finding: Go has huge branching and no good handcrafted evaluation, so alpha-beta stalled and MCTS took over; in chess alpha-beta with strong evaluation stayed on top until neural-guided MCTS and NNUE.
numbers: Survey: top MCTS Go programs about good amateur strength in 2011. Then AlphaGo 5-0 (Fan Hui) and 4-1 (Lee Sedol). AlphaZero 2017 chess vs alpha-beta: 28W 72D 0L over 100 games.
limits: Interpretive link across two documents; the survey does not discuss chess head to head.
agent_relevance: Choose search type by branching factor and by whether a trustworthy evaluator exists. For open-ended LLM tasks, branching is large and evaluators are weak, so soft best-first search is the better analogue.

source: AlphaZero scaling with thinking time (Fig 2) and the alpha-beta belief
finding: AlphaZero's MCTS scaled better with thinking time than Stockfish or Elmo, challenging the belief that alpha-beta is inherently better.
numbers: AlphaZero 80 thousand positions per second in chess and 40 thousand in shogi vs 70 million for Stockfish and 35 million for Elmo. Elo plotted against Stockfish or Elmo at 40 ms thinking time.
quote: calling into question the widely held belief that alpha-beta search is inherently superior in these domains
limits: Footnote: draws compress the chess Elo scale. One lab's runs; tuning of rivals at long time controls not independently checked in the preprint.
agent_relevance: With a good prior, selective search can turn extra compute into strength more efficiently than uniform wide search.

source: AlphaGo v Lee Sedol (2016) game 4: a Monte Carlo value collapse (via Wikipedia)
finding: In the one game AlphaGo lost, a surprise move by Lee Sedol led AlphaGo's win estimate to collapse and its play to degrade.
numbers: Match 4-1 to AlphaGo (9-15 March 2016). Lee's white move 78 was a brilliant tesuji. AlphaGo estimated about 70% at move 79; the estimate dropped suddenly at move 87; very bad moves followed from 87 to 101. AlphaGo resigned when its win estimate fell below 20%.
limits: Secondary source; the cause (typical Monte Carlo error) is one commentator's view, not a verified analysis.
agent_relevance: A low-probability line that the search never expanded can wreck the estimate. A scaffold should keep a cheap check for 'the opponent has a surprising reply' before trusting a high score.

source: Jones (2021) Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games: board-size frontier
finding: Compute frontiers in Hex are exponential in target performance, and small-board runs predict large-board frontiers.
numbers: Error in the frontier prediction drops exponentially as more small board sizes are added to the fit. Exact exponents not extracted.
limits: One game, one algorithm (AlphaZero on Hex).
agent_relevance: The cost of strong search grows fast with problem size. Budget depth explicitly and use cheap small-instance pilots to set the budget.
